problem: Consider the section of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ that lies in the second quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{3}$ on the circle at the point where $x=-\sqrt{3},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{3}$ and $x=-\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot (-\sqrt{3}))+(\sqrt{3})\cdot (2y) & =0. \\ -2\sqrt{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2\sqrt{3}y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-\sqrt{3}$ into the equation of the circle.

At the point where $x=-\sqrt{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {(-\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ 3+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second 
quadrant.

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
